conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way. We’ll use a brief, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply 10 questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days, and it helps us spot anything that might benefit from extra support. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the small team directly involved in your care.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories. If any question feels hard to answer, just say what feels closest to your experience. We’ll go at your pace, and we can pause whenever you need. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?
Honestly, I have laughed a little—like when my partner made a silly face at the baby—but it feels forced. Most of the time humor just slides past me; nothing feels very funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I can manage a tiny laugh if someone else is joking, but it doesn’t feel natural or lift my mood.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still try to plan little things—like a walk with the baby or my favorite show—but when the moment comes, the spark just isn’t there. I go through the motions, but it feels flat, like I’m watching myself from far away.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself thinking it’s my fault whenever the baby fusses for a long time or won’t settle. I keep replaying what I did—“Maybe I didn’t feed him right,” or “I must be missing something obvious”—even when everyone says babies just cry. I know in my head it’s not rational, but the guilt still shows up most days.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s fine, but my chest feels tight and my mind races—what if he stops breathing, what if I’m doing everything wrong? There’s no real reason, but I can’t switch the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times this week. It comes out of nowhere—my heart starts racing, I feel shaky, and I have to check the baby’s breathing or pace the hallway. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me drained.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the dishes, the laundry, the feeds, the night-wakings all pile up faster than I can clear them. I’ll be folding onesies and suddenly feel like I’m drowning—like I can’t come up for air. I still manage, but it takes way more effort than it used to.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t quiet down—kept replaying everything I might have messed up that day. I finally drift off, then I wake up at two or three a.m. with my heart pounding, sure I heard the baby or forgot something important. It takes forever to settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. There’s this heavy, gray feeling that sits on me from the moment I open my eyes. Sometimes it lightens a little if the baby smiles, but it always settles back in. I keep thinking, “I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’ve got support,” but the sadness just lingers.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… a couple of times this week it just bubbled over. Once was after a night when the baby wouldn’t settle and I finally got him down, then I looked at the mess around me and the tears came. Another time my mom asked how I was doing and I couldn’t even answer—I just stood there crying over the sink.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I’ve had a couple of quick flashes—like “what if I just kept driving past the house and didn’t come back,” or a picture of the pill bottle jumping into my head—but they’re gone as fast as they show up. I don’t want to die; I just want the pressure to stop. I haven’t made any plans and I’m pretty sure I wouldn’t act on them, but yeah, the thoughts have popped in this week.

You've courageously shared that since your baby's arrival most days feel heavy and gray: joy and laughter rarely come naturally, worry and panic surface without warning, and simple tasks feel overwhelming. You describe nightly insomnia driven by racing thoughts, frequent tearfulness, guilt when your baby fusses, and fleeting images of escape. These feelings persist despite having support and a healthy infant, leaving you exhausted and frightened by your own thoughts.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no ability to laugh naturally; "tiny laugh" only with effort maps to "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes anhedonia—loss of pleasure and emotional engagement despite attempts to plan enjoyable activities—matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent self-blame occurring "most days" when baby fusses, fitting "Yes, some of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, uncontrollable worry without external cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple discrete panic episodes this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" and uses vivid metaphors of drowning and piling tasks, indicating intermittent difficulty coping, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption due to racing thoughts and nocturnal awakenings, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "pretty much every day" and a pervasive "heavy, gray feeling" that dominates her waking life, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct crying episodes triggered by stress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, brief intrusive thoughts of self-harm (driving past home, pill bottle image) that resolve quickly, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 25 falls well above the ≥14 threshold for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> and a Q10 score ≥1 mandates urgent follow-up. You endorse core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days (<sym>heavy gray feeling</sym>), markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>spark isn't there</sym>), significant weight/appetite change not assessed, insomnia nearly every night, psychomotor agitation (<sym>pacing the hallway</sym>), fatigue, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt (<sym>everything is my fault</sym>), diminished concentration, and recurrent thoughts of death. Daily <sym>anxiety</sym> and panic symptoms suggest a likely comorbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. Frequency, duration (daily, past week), and functional impact (feels drowning, impaired sleep) indicate moderate-severity episode with elevated safety risk. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for full evaluation and safety plan
2. Call 988 (U.S.) or your local mental-health crisis line if thoughts of harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Inform a trusted adult nearby about these thoughts so you're not alone with them
4. Schedule brief daily check-ins with your support person to rate mood/anxiety 0-10 and track any safety concerns
5. Begin basic <sym>sleep-hygiene</sym>: 30 min wind-down, dim lights, no screens, delegate one night-feed to partner if possible
6. Consider referral to a therapist trained in <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression</med>; start within one week
7. Discuss with provider whether an <med>SSRI</med> compatible with breastfeeding is indicated
8. Arrange practical help-meal train, cleaning support, or relative staying over-to reduce overwhelming tasks
9. Attend a local new-mother support group or virtual PPD group; peer contact reduces isolation
10. Follow up with this office within 48-72 h to confirm appointment attendance and review safety plan
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Affect/mood: Persistent dysphoria described as “heavy, gray feeling” present daily.  
Anhedonia: Marked loss of enjoyment—“spark isn’t there,” “watching myself from far away.”  
Appetite/weight: Not assessed.  
Sleep: Initial and middle insomnia linked to ruminative guilt; wakes 2–3 a.m. with anxiety.  
Energy/coping: Feels “drowning” in routine tasks; effort to complete basic care.  
Cognition: Excessive self-blame (“everything is my fault”) despite objective reassurance.  
Anxiety: Daily free-floating worry, tight chest, multiple panic episodes this week.  
Psychotic features: Denied.  
Trauma/obsessions: Intrusive catastrophic thoughts of infant harm.  
Self-harm: Fleeting passive suicidal ideation (driving past home, pill-bottle image) without intent or plan; transient desire to “stop the pressure.”  
Infant-related: Guilt intensifies when baby fusses; frequent checking of breathing.

Pattern: Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive and anxious symptoms of 1–2 weeks’ duration, functional impairment, and passive suicidal ideation.

Risk flags:  
• Passive suicidal thoughts (no plan)  
• Daily panic symptoms  
• Impaired sleep secondary to mood  
• Overwhelmed coping capacity

Screening conclusion: Positive screen for postpartum depression/anxiety with elevated safety risk; warrants same-day clinician review for comprehensive assessment, safety plan, and discussion of supports/resources.
